options.text: The tiny gap between two neurones
options.explanation: A synapse is the microscopic gap separating neurones.
Neurones are not directly connected — the gap is the point.
Neurotransmitters cross the synapse; they are not it.
That describes a nerve.

questions.stem: What triggers the release of neurotransmitters?

options.text: The next neurone pulling chemicals across
options.explanation: Diffusion carries the chemicals; nothing pulls them.

options.text: An electrical impulse reaching the end of a neurone
options.explanation: The arriving impulse triggers the chemical release.
Blood flow plays no role in the synapse.
Light is an external stimulus, not the synaptic trigger.

questions.stem: How do neurotransmitters cross the synapse?

options.explanation: Molecules do not swim; diffusion does the work.

options.text: Through hollow tubes joining the cells
options.explanation: No tubes connect the neurones.
Neurotransmitters diffuse across the synapse.

options.text: As electrical impulses jumping the gap
options.explanation: The electrical impulse stops at the gap; chemicals finish the trip.

questions.stem: What happens when neurotransmitters bind to the next neurone?

options.text: The next neurone stores them forever
options.explanation: Binding triggers a signal, not storage.
The gap remains open for future transmissions.
The whole point of the relay is to continue the message.

options.text: A new electrical impulse is generated
options.explanation: Binding sparks a fresh impulse in the next cell.

questions.stem: Why is a chemical handover needed between two neurones?

options.text: Because the two neurones never actually touch — a gap always separates them
options.explanation: The physical gap forces the chemical relay.
Speed is an advantage, not a problem.

options.text: Because impulses are too large to fit
options.explanation: Impulses have no size in that sense.
Meaningless — molecules do not exercise.

questions.stem: Define a synapse and name the chemicals that cross it.
questions.modelAnswer: The tiny gap between two neurones, crossed by chemical messengers called neurotransmitters.

questions.stem: State the full handover sequence at a synapse.
questions.modelAnswer: Impulse arrives, neurotransmitters are released, they diffuse across the synapse, they bind to the next neurone, and a new impulse is generated.

questions.stem: Explain why the electrical impulse itself cannot simply continue across the synapse.
questions.modelAnswer: The two neurones are separate cells with a real gap between them, so there is no continuous membrane for the electrical signal to travel along; the signal must be converted to chemical form, diffused across, and regenerated as a fresh impulse in the next cell.

questions.stem: A poison blocks neurotransmitter release at one synapse in a reflex arc. Predict the effect on the response and justify it.
questions.modelAnswer: The response fails: with neurotransmitters blocked, the signal cannot cross that synapse, so no new impulse is generated in the next neurone and the message never reaches the effector — the chain is broken even though every other neurone works.
